text: Abstract—Drought impacts depend not only on lost monsoon rainfall but also on a district's reliance on rain-fed agriculture and its capacity to cope. This paper presents an exploratory composite index of relative El Niño drought vulnerability for 34 districts of Maharashtra, India. Six indicators were built from official sources: the sensitivity of June to September rainfall to the Relative Oceanic Niño Index and the frequency of deficient monsoons in 18 El Niño years, from India Meteorological Department gridded rainfall for 1950 to 2024; agricultural-worker share and literacy from Census 2011; rainfed share of net sown area from the Census 2011 Village Directory; and small-holding share from the Agriculture Census 2010-11. After direction alignment and standardization, principal component analysis was used only to derive indicator weights, from the absolute loadings of three retained components (74.5 percent of variance) weighted by explained variance. The weighted sum was rescaled to a relative 0 to 100 index, and K-Means clustering of the index (K = 3) identified 10 High, 20 Medium and 4 Low vulnerability districts, with the High group concentrated in Marathwada. The weights were close to equal (0.151 to 0.183), consistent with a low Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value of 0.40, and rankings were stable across six alternative specifications (rank correlation 0.934 to 0.995). The index showed a moderate positive association with the share of talukas declared drought-affected by the state government in 2018 (Spearman 0.585), 2023 (0.450) and a 2026 holdout (0.545), offering a transparent basis for district-level drought preparedness screening.

text: Drought is a recurring hazard whose impacts arise from the interaction between a rainfall deficit and the agricultural and social systems that the deficit affects [1], [2]. In India, kharif agriculture depends heavily on the June to September southwest monsoon, and year-to-year monsoon variability is reflected in crop production [3]. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is one of the main external influences on this variability. Warm El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific have historically been associated with below-normal Indian monsoon rainfall [4], [5], although the relationship has varied over time and not every El Niño year produces a drought [5], [6].

text: Maharashtra shows why rainfall alone is an incomplete guide to drought impact. Recurring drought is a major challenge in its drought-prone areas, where agriculture, including rainfed cropping and livestock, is the main income activity of much of the population [7]. A 50-year district study of the state found that some districts were vulnerable despite low exposure to climate variability, because of their sensitivity and adaptive-capacity characteristics [8]. This agrees with the widely used view of vulnerability as a function of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity [9], [10]. A district assessment therefore has to combine climate exposure with agricultural dependence, irrigation status, landholding structure and socioeconomic capacity.

text: Combining such indicators requires weights. Expert-based schemes such as the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) are common in Indian drought studies but rest on subjective judgments [11], [12], while equal weighting ignores the overlap between indicators. Multivariate methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) provide data-driven weights, but they need care: component signs are arbitrary, and with few spatial units the estimated structure can be unstable [13], [14]. In addition, few district studies link vulnerability explicitly to El Niño-specific rainfall behaviour or test their output against independent administrative drought records.

text: Vulnerability research separates the hazard from the characteristics of the exposed system that shape its consequences [10], [15]. Indicator-based assessments put this into practice through exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity, a structure taken from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Third Assessment Report [9] and widely applied to agricultural drought [2], [16].

text: Indian studies have applied this structure at several scales. Murthy et al. [16] built a composite agricultural drought vulnerability index from exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity using geospatial data, and Sharma and Ravindranath [17] applied the IPCC 2014 framework to hazard-specific vulnerability assessment. Chakraborty and Joshi [11] mapped the disaster vulnerability of Indian districts with AHP, and Saha et al. [12] combined fuzzy logic with AHP to map drought vulnerability in Odisha. Within Maharashtra, Nair and Mirajkar [18] assessed drought vulnerability across the Vidarbha region, and Swami and Parthasarathy [8] aggregated district indicators with equal weights over 1966 to 2015. These studies show the value of combining physical and social indicators, but they mostly rely on expert or equal weights, and their climate exposure is generally not tied to ENSO.

text: Statistical weighting through PCA or factor analysis is a recognised option for composite indicators [13]. Cutter et al. [19] used factor analysis to construct the Social Vulnerability Index, and Abson et al. [20] used PCA for socio-ecological vulnerability mapping in Southern Africa. Balaganesh et al. [21] derived PCA weights for a composite drought vulnerability index of Tamil Nadu districts and classified the districts by index magnitude. Kim et al. [22] combined PCA with a Gaussian mixture model to assess regional drought vulnerability and risk in South Korea, and Pinzón Flórez et al. [23] derived indicator weights from eigenvalues and absolute loadings for a territorial composite vulnerability index. The composite-indicator handbook of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) notes that PCA-based weights depend on correlation among the indicators and are sensitive to small samples, which is why factorability is usually checked with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure [24] and Bartlett's test before such weights are used [13].

text: Cluster analysis has also been used to group spatial units into vulnerability classes, for example K-Means classification of social vulnerability [25]. K-Means [26] partitions observations by minimizing the within-cluster sum of squared distances. When it is applied to a single index, it places class boundaries at natural gaps in the values rather than at fixed cut-offs.

text: Compared with this literature, the present study (i) derives exposure specifically from the El Niño behaviour of long gridded rainfall records using the current official ENSO index of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), (ii) uses sign-safe PCA weights with explicit factorability, retention and stability diagnostics, (iii) applies clustering only after the index has been constructed, and (iv) evaluates the result against administrative drought declarations that were never used in constructing the index, including a holdout year.

text: The study area is Maharashtra in its current administrative form of 36 districts. Palghar, which was separated from Thane after the 2011 Census, was reconstructed from its eight Census 2011 sub-districts in every source. Mumbai City and Mumbai Suburban have no villages in the Census 2011 Village Directory and no holdings in the Agriculture Census report, so the agricultural and landholding indicators do not exist for them. They were excluded from the index, which therefore covers 34 districts. All tables were joined on numeric Census 2011 and Local Government Directory district codes, and names were never used as join keys. Renamed districts (Ahilyanagar, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Dharashiv) keep their original codes.

text: Climate data were taken from the IMD 0.25 × 0.25 degree gridded daily rainfall product [27] for 1950 to 2024, the primary study period. The ENSO index is the NOAA Climate Prediction Center's RONI, which compares the Niño-3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly with the tropical-mean anomaly so that background warming does not inflate it [28]. RONI values were taken from NOAA's published series [29], and RONI became NOAA's official ENSO index in February 2026 [30]. The conventional Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) was used only as a sensitivity check.

text: Two data-quality issues were handled without editing the raw files. In the Village Directory, the columns labelled irrigated and unirrigated area are interchanged: the source-wise irrigated areas sum to the column labelled unirrigated in 43,661 of 43,665 villages, so the processing code maps the columns explicitly. In the IMD grid, ten district-years exceed twice the district baseline, for example Pune in 2005 (4.87 times) and 2009 (2.03 times). No published correction was found, so all published values were kept in the primary analysis and a version excluding Pune's two flagged years was computed for sensitivity only. No values were imputed.

text: Warm ENSO seasons were identified with NOAA's rule: the three-month index, rounded to 0.1 °C, is at least +0.5 °C for at least five consecutive overlapping seasons. The implementation reproduced all 919 seasons of NOAA's published ONI table and 915 of 919 seasons of the RONI table; the four differences lie in a 1984 La Niña run and affect no El Niño season. A year was treated as an El Niño monsoon year when both the June to August and July to September seasons fell inside a warm episode. This gave 18 El Niño monsoon years under RONI between 1950 and 2024.

The resulting six indicators in Table I cover exposure (the two ENSO indicators), sensitivity (agricultural-worker share, rainfed share and small-holding share) and adaptive capacity (literacy). The largest absolute correlation between any two of them is 0.45. The direction of each indicator is an assumption of the exposure, sensitivity and adaptive-capacity framework and is not tested by this study.

text: The number of retained components was chosen with the Kaiser rule (eigenvalue above 1) [40], the OECD and JRC practice of eigenvalues above 1, each component above 10 percent and a cumulative share above 60 percent, and the Jolliffe threshold of 0.7, both as described in the handbook [13]. text: Absolute loadings are used because the sign of a principal component is arbitrary, whereas the direction of each indicator is fixed by the framework through the alignment step. In these data, the small-holding share loads opposite to the other strong indicators on the first component, so signed aggregation of components would give it a negative weight and contradict its stated direction. The absolute-loading form lets PCA determine how much each indicator counts, while alignment determines which way it counts. The resulting weights are exploratory statistical weights and do not represent theoretical importance.

text: where di,t is the number of talukas declared in the main Government Resolution (GR) and Ti is the number of Census 2011 talukas (355 in total). For 2018 and 2023 the numerator counts severe and moderate talukas in the final declaration; for 2026 it counts Trigger-1 talukas. text: The six indicators share little common structure. The KMO measure is 0.40, below the 0.6 usually recommended for PCA-based weighting [13], although Bartlett's test rejects an identity correlation matrix (χ² = 35.5, 15 degrees of freedom, p = 0.002). This is largely a consequence of feature selection, which removed redundant indicators. It means that the data contain weak common-factor structure, so the PCA-derived weights should be interpreted as exploratory statistical weights rather than as evidence of a strong latent vulnerability construct.

text: Table II and Fig. 2 show that three components have eigenvalues above 1 and together explain 74.5 percent of the variance, so the Kaiser, OECD and JRC, and Jolliffe rules all retain three. Horn's parallel analysis retains only PC1, the only eigenvalue clearly above the random-data benchmark, which reflects the uncertainty of a 34-district sample. The leave-one-district-out analysis supports PC1: its direction barely changes (median absolute cosine 0.999; minimum 0.948 when Pune is omitted). PC2 and PC3 have close eigenvalues and can swap order when Pune or Ratnagiri is omitted, but the plane they span remains stable (projection of at least 0.926).

text: Table V shows that the district ordering is robust. Every alternative has a Spearman correlation of at least 0.934 with the primary index, and all but the OECD and JRC version are at or above 0.961. At most four of the 34 districts change group, and no district moves between Low and High in any version. The districts that change are close to a group boundary, for example Wardha (32.6), Hingoli (65.9), Washim (62.7) and Buldhana (61.2), and their classification should be treated as less certain. The very high agreement with equal weights (0.993) confirms that the ranking does not hinge on the precise PCA weights. Excluding Pune's two flagged rainfall years lowers Pune's index from 37.3 to 35.3 and leaves the ranking almost unchanged. The OECD and JRC method differs most because it rewards indicators that belong clearly to a single rotated factor, which gives the ENSO slope a low weight (0.092). With ONI instead of RONI, Jalna rather than Beed has the highest index.

text: Table VI and Fig. 6 show that the index has a moderate positive association with the declared taluka share in all three years. In 2018, the most informative year with 26 districts declared, districts with higher index values tended to have a larger share of talukas declared (ρ = 0.585). The association is weaker in 2023 (ρ = 0.450), when the main GR covered only 40 talukas and the remaining declarations were made by revenue circle. In the 2026 holdout, the fixed index and groups show an association of similar strength (ρ = 0.545). In every year the mean declared share rises from the Low group to the Medium and High groups.

text: Overall, the validation is consistent with the index capturing relative drought vulnerability. Only 2023 was an El Niño monsoon year under the RONI rule, so the validation tests general correspondence with drought declarations rather than El Niño-driven drought alone. text: The study has several limitations. First, the primary index covers only 34 districts, which limits statistical power; parallel analysis retains only one component, and the second and third components are not separately stable. Second, the KMO value of 0.40 indicates weak common-factor structure, so the weights are exploratory and close to equal weighting, and the small-holding share is negatively correlated with the other aligned indicators, so its direction is set by the framework rather than shown by the data. Third, the socioeconomic and agricultural indicators refer to 2011 and 2010-11 and are combined with current Survey of India boundaries, and adaptive capacity is represented only by literacy because no verified district data on income, credit or infrastructure were available. Fourth, some published IMD rainfall values, notably Pune's in 2005 and 2009, are implausibly high; they were kept as published, and whether they are errors could not be verified. Fifth, drought declarations are administrative decisions rather than direct observations of crop loss: the 2023 taluka list captures only part of that year's declarations, and the 2026 holdout is an early Trigger-1 stage in which 19 of 34 districts were fully declared, which limits discrimination. Finally, the 0 to 100 index is relative to the districts studied, and the analysis identifies associations rather than causal effects.

text: This study developed an exploratory composite index of relative El Niño drought vulnerability for 34 districts of Maharashtra by combining two El Niño-specific rainfall indicators with four agricultural and socioeconomic indicators. PCA was used to derive sign-safe weights from absolute loadings, the weighted sum was rescaled to a relative 0 to 100 index, and K-Means grouped the districts into 10 High, 20 Medium and 4 Low vulnerability districts. The highest vulnerability is concentrated in Marathwada and the adjoining dry interior, where large El Niño rainfall losses coincide with high agricultural dependence and lower literacy. The weights were close to equal, the ranking was stable across six alternative specifications, and the index showed a moderate positive association with drought declarations in 2018, 2023 and a 2026 holdout. The framework is transparent and reproducible and can support district-level screening for drought preparedness, provided its relative and exploratory nature is respected.
